blocks.text: A strain-gauge bridge on a crane hook produces only a few millivolts, far too little for a data logger. A single op-amp and two resistors turn that signal into a clean, scaled voltage whose gain is fixed to within a fraction of a percent by the resistor ratio, regardless of how the amplifier chip itself varies from batch to batch.

blocks.markdown: An **operational amplifier** (op-amp) is a high-gain differential amplifier with two inputs, the non-inverting input $(+)$ and the inverting input $(-)$, and one output. Its output is $v_o=A\,(v_+-v_-)$, where the open-loop gain $A$ is very large (typically $10^5$ or more) but poorly controlled. It is therefore never used bare for linear amplification; it is used with **negative feedback**, which makes the overall gain depend only on the external resistors.

blocks.title: Ideal op-amp rules (with negative feedback)
blocks.text: 1. The inputs draw no current (infinite input impedance): $i_+=i_-=0$. 2. The feedback forces the two input voltages to be equal: $v_+=v_-$ (the **virtual short**), provided the output is not saturated. 3. The output can supply whatever current is needed, up to the supply limits.

blocks.markdown: Rule 2 follows from rearranging $v_o=A(v_+-v_-)$: since $v_o$ is finite (limited by the supplies, say $\pm12$ V) and $A$ is huge, the difference $v_+-v_-=v_o/A$ is a few microvolts at most, and is taken as zero. Rule 1 follows from the very large input resistance of the input transistors. These two rules are enough to analyse nearly every op-amp circuit.

**Inverting amplifier.** The input source drives the inverting node through $R_{in}$, the feedback resistor $R_f$ connects the output back to that node, and the $(+)$ input is grounded. By the virtual short the $(-)$ node is at 0 V (a 'virtual ground'), so the input current is $v_{in}/R_{in}$. That current cannot enter the op-amp (rule 1), so it flows through $R_f$, giving $v_o=-R_f\,v_{in}/R_{in}$.

blocks.title: Inverting amplifier
blocks.prompt: An inverting amplifier uses $R_{in}=10$ k$\Omega$ and $R_f=47$ k$\Omega$. The input is +0.20 V. Find the gain and the output voltage.

steps.text: Virtual ground puts 0 V at the inverting node, so the input current is:
The same current flows through $R_f$ (no current enters the op-amp), so:

blocks.answer: Gain -4.7; the output is -0.94 V. The sign inversion is a 180 degree phase shift.

blocks.markdown: **Non-inverting amplifier.** The input source drives the $(+)$ input directly. A voltage divider $R_f$, $R_g$ from the output to ground feeds a fraction $\beta=R_g/(R_g+R_f)$ of the output back to the $(-)$ input. The virtual short forces $v_-=v_{in}$, so $v_o\beta=v_{in}$, giving the gain $1/\beta=1+R_f/R_g$. Its input resistance is essentially infinite, which makes it ideal for high-impedance sensors; the gain is never below 1.

blocks.title: Non-inverting amplifier design
blocks.prompt: Design a non-inverting amplifier with gain 10 from a 0.25 V input, with $R_g=10$ k$\Omega$. Find $R_f$ and the output.

steps.text: Check the gain with the chosen standard values (90 k is not E12; use 91 k).

blocks.answer: Use $R_f=91$ k$\Omega$ (nearest standard value) for a gain of 10.1 and an output of 2.53 V, comfortably inside a +/-12 V supply.

blocks.markdown: **Role of feedback.** With a finite open-loop gain $A$ and feedback fraction $\beta$, the closed-loop gain of the non-inverting stage is $G=A/(1+A\beta)$. When $A\beta\gg1$ this becomes $G\approx1/\beta$, independent of $A$. Negative feedback therefore trades the huge, unpredictable gain $A$ for a smaller, precise gain set by resistor ratios; it also reduces distortion and widens the bandwidth. If the output were connected to the $(+)$ input instead (positive feedback), any small difference would be amplified further and the output would saturate at a supply rail.

Inverting gain $-R_f/R_{in}$; non-inverting gain $1+R_f/R_g$; choose resistor values to meet a gain.
Negative feedback makes $G\approx1/\beta$ independent of the open-loop gain $A$.

questions.stem: An inverting amplifier has $R_{in}=4.7$ k$\Omega$ and $R_f=47$ k$\Omega$. What is its gain?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this drops the inversion sign.

questions.explanation: The inverting gain is $-R_f/R_{in}=-47/4.7=-10$. The negative sign means the output is inverted relative to the input.

questions.stem: A non-inverting amplifier has $R_f=20$ k$\Omega$ and $R_g=5$ k$\Omega$. What is its gain?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 4 is Rf/Rg and forgets the added 1.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the inverting form.

questions.explanation: The non-inverting gain is $1+R_f/R_g=1+20/5=5$. The '1' arises because the input voltage appears at the inverting node and the output must exceed it by the divider fraction.

questions.stem: What does negative feedback achieve in an op-amp amplifier?

options.text: It makes the closed-loop gain depend mainly on external resistor ratios rather than on the open-loop gain
It makes the output independent of the input
It removes the need for a power supply

questions.correctOptionText: It makes the closed-loop gain depend mainly on external resistor ratios rather than on the open-loop gain

distractorRationale.a: Correct: with A large, G is approximately 1/beta.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: feedback reduces the overall gain from A to about 1/beta.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the output still follows the input, at the gain set by the resistors.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the op-amp still needs supply rails.

questions.explanation: Negative feedback returns a fraction $\beta$ of the output to the inverting input, forcing the closed-loop gain to $\approx1/\beta$. The huge but uncertain $A$ drops out of the result.

questions.stem: An inverting amplifier with $R_{in}=2.2$ k$\Omega$ must have a gain of -25. Which value of $R_f$ is needed?

distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this uses (G - 1) x R_in, the non-inverting formula.

questions.explanation: The inverting gain is $-R_f/R_{in}$, so $R_f=25\times2.2=55$ k$\Omega$. The non-inverting form would need $(G-1)R_g$, which is a different circuit.

questions.stem: Which statement about input resistance is correct for ideal single op-amp amplifiers?

options.text: Inverting: input resistance equals R_in; non-inverting: very large
Inverting: very large; non-inverting: equals R_g
Both equal the feedback resistor R_f

questions.correctOptionText: Inverting: input resistance equals R_in; non-inverting: very large

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the inverting node is a virtual ground, so the source sees R_in; the (+) input draws no current.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the inverting source drives current into R_in.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: reversed; the inverting source sees R_in.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: R_f is not directly the source load in either circuit.

questions.explanation: In the inverting amplifier the source drives $R_{in}$ with the other end at virtual ground, so it supplies current $v_{in}/R_{in}$. In the non-inverting circuit the source connects only to the op-amp input, which draws no current.

questions.stem: An inverting amplifier has $R_{in}=15$ k$\Omega$ and $R_f=68$ k$\Omega$. The input voltage is -0.35 V. What is the output voltage in volts?
questions.explanation: The gain is $-68/15=-4.533$. Output $=-4.533\times(-0.35)=+1.587$ V. The two negative signs make the output positive.

questions.stem: A non-inverting amplifier with $R_g=2.2$ k$\Omega$ is to have a gain of 21. What value of $R_f$ is needed, in k$\Omega$?
questions.explanation: From $G=1+R_f/R_g$, $R_f=(G-1)R_g=20\times2.2=44$ k$\Omega$. A standard 43 k$\Omega$ (1 %) would give gain 20.5.

questions.stem: A non-inverting amplifier has $R_f=99$ k$\Omega$ and $R_g=1.0$ k$\Omega$ (ideal gain 100). The op-amp's actual open-loop gain is only $A=1000$. Using $G=A/(1+A\beta)$ with $\beta=R_g/(R_g+R_f)$, find the actual closed-loop gain.
questions.explanation: $\beta=1/(1+99)=0.01$, so $A\beta=10$ and $G=1000/(1+10)=90.9$. The ideal value of 100 is only approached when $A\beta\gg1$; here the gain is about 9 % low.

questions.stem: Using the ideal op-amp rules, derive the gain of the inverting amplifier from first principles.
markingGuide: States virtual short: v_- = v_+ = 0 (virtual ground)
No current enters the op-amp input, so the same current flows through R_f
questions.explanation: With the $(+)$ input grounded and the virtual short, the inverting node is at 0 V. The input current is $v_{in}/R_{in}$, and since the op-amp draws no input current it all flows through $R_f$. The output is thus $v_o=0-iR_f=-(R_f/R_{in})v_{in}$.

questions.stem: Explain why an op-amp amplifier uses negative rather than positive feedback, and why with negative feedback the closed-loop gain is almost independent of the op-amp's open-loop gain.
markingGuide: Negative feedback returns a fraction beta of the output to the inverting input
Any difference v_+ - v_- is reduced because the output moves to oppose it (self-correcting)
Closed-loop gain G = A/(1+A beta) approaches 1/beta when A beta is much greater than 1
So gain depends on the resistor ratio, not on A which varies with temperature and batch
Positive feedback amplifies the difference further, driving the output to saturate (unstable for linear amplification)
questions.explanation: With negative feedback, if the output rises too far the fed-back signal reduces the differential input and pulls the output back, so the circuit settles where $v_+\approx v_-$. Algebraically $G=A/(1+A\beta)\to1/\beta$ for large $A\beta$, so the gain depends on resistor values, not on $A$. Positive feedback would amplify any small imbalance and drive the output into saturation.
